[MATH: {5u − 6v = 3; − 3u + 2v = − 5]

sections.normalized_html:
Notice that the [MATH: v]-coefficient in the first equation is [MATH: -6,] while in the second equation it is [MATH: 2.]

If we multiply the second equation by [MATH: 3,] then the [MATH: v]-coefficient will become [MATH: 6,] which will cancel with the coefficient of [MATH: -6] in the first equation. [MATH: {5u − 6v = 3; (− 3u + 2v = − 5) × (3)]

Now, when we add the two equations, the variable [MATH: v] will be eliminated: [MATH: 5u − 6v|= 3; − 9u + 6v|= − 15; (5u − 9u)|= (3 − 15); − 4u|= − 12; u|= 3]

So, the solution must have [MATH: u = 3.] However, we still need to find [MATH: v.] To do this, we substitute [MATH: u = 3] back into one of the equations. Let's choose the second equation: [MATH: − 3u + 2v|= − 5; − 3(3) + 2v|= − 5; − 9 + 2v|= − 5; 2v|= 4; v|= 2]

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is [MATH: u = 3, \,v = 2,] which can be expressed as [MATH: (3,2).]
